extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and judging school- and nation-level physical training and education systems that promote bodily and nervous development, public health, and practical preparedness. Compares different training philosophies (German turning, Swedish movement, English sport) and lists physical/health criteria schools should address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise must train both muscles and the central nervous system
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical culture is not only exercise of the muscles but quite as much, yes, more, exercise of the gray substance of the central nerve-system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design programs so they develop composite movements and neural coordination (concatenations in ganglion-cells), not merely isolated muscle strength. Beware programs that only strengthen single muscles (see Swedish movement limitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match training form to practical ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If the end is masterhood in running, jumping, climbing, dancing, fencing, riding, swimming, rowing, or skating, then practice directly the necessary concatenations in actions without pausing at theoretical preliminary steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose English-style sports/practical activities for direct skill mastery. Conversely, if broad, general preparedness is the goal, select systematic methods (e.g., German turning) that teach learning-to-learn and a wide repertoire of movements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swedish movement is limited to single-muscle strengthening and therapeutic use
rubrics_metrics.description: The physiological value of the Swedish movement is that it can strengthen the muscles, but has not power to make composite movements fluent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve Swedish/simple-resistance movements for physicians' purposes (to keep up or restore efficiency of single muscle groups), not as the main curriculum for healthy youth aiming at complex motor skills.

rubrics_metrics.name: German turning provides broad, equable bodily perfecting and learning methods
rubrics_metrics.description: German turning furnishes opportunity for exercise with small external preparations, implies moral earnestness of self-improvement, and through ingenious selection of exercises results in a more equable perfecting of the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use German-style systematic gymnastics to give youth 'ready forms of movement for every situation'—valuable for inclusivity and for teaching transferable motor methods. It also allows progression into practical forms; avoid conflating it with 'order-exercises'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-reliance on order-exercises (kindergarten-level drills) as main preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The so-called order-exercises, over-estimated as preparatives to exercising, and a lazy-bench for inefficient teachers of turning, belong to the Kindergarten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure primary curricula emphasize meaningful motor skills and varied physical play rather than rote marching/drill exercises that add little practical motor ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical education must be inclusive and require minimal external preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: German turning offers the advantage of furnishing to any number of youth, of every age and condition, opportunity for exercise with the smallest amount of external preparations, and independent of often unattainable external conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design school programs that are feasible in varied resource settings so all children can participate; prioritize exercises that do not depend on expensive facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: National education should combine elementary literacy with systematic physical training
rubrics_metrics.description: Elementary practices of learning to read, write, and calculate are necessities, but are comparatively valueless unless combined with further necessities of a physical kind — namely, sound and systematic muscular training; freedom of breathing, and circulation of the blood; practical training... readiness to acquire any craft or handicraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate curriculum time and some budget from 'mental-only' teaching toward physical training, singing, swimming, graceful walking, and manual skills to produce well-rounded, employable citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against excessive mental pressure without physical training
rubrics_metrics.description: Undue nervous exhaustion and confinement are supplied by over-mental work without physical training and so fatal diseases (e.g., phthisis) are systematically fanned from latency into activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the school day with play and outdoor exercise; monitor workloads to prevent chronic fatigue, anemia, cachexia, and other nutrition-related conditions exacerbated by confinement and overwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use exercise as a preventive and remedial measure for common constitutional conditions in schoolchildren
rubrics_metrics.description: The one saving clause in many affected children was development by physical training, and that was withheld. Preventives for consumption and nervous exhaustion are freedom from nervous exhaustion combined with physical exercise in open breathing-space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include outdoor breathing-space activities and systematic physical conditioning in school health policy to prevent/treat anemia, cachexia, scrofula, early consumptive tendencies, spinal deformities, and poor muscular/skeletal development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor training progress with empirical measures; expect non-linear improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Fechner's curves of daily exercise showed that at first the exercise appeared to bear no fruit, then results came all at once, but soon reached their limit; the curves do not rise steadily but in a serrated manner according as weariness or increasing facility prevailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When inspecting recruits or tracking pupil improvement, collect empirical performance/ fatigue data over time; anticipate serrated (stepwise) gains and plateaus, and adjust regimen and rest accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design training to promote transferable motor learning (learning-to-learn)
rubrics_metrics.description: The youthful body, thoroughly trained after the German method, enjoys the extraordinary advantage that, like a well-instructed mathematician, it is provided with methods for every problem... Nothing prevents the German turner at pleasure carrying his more theoretical training into practical and immediately available forms of exercise, in which he, since he has learned to learn, speedily attains the skill which his natural ability permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pedagogical elements that teach how to learn physical skills so students can rapidly acquire new practical activities; mix theory and practice sensibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume transmission of acquired bodily properties without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificially acquired changes do not necessarily become hereditary; transmission of acquired properties is obscure and incomprehensible; one should not adopt 'unconscious recollection' or similar analogies as explanatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing curriculum or public-health policy on the unproven assertion that improved traits gained by training will be inherited; ground arguments in observable, mechanistic evidence rather than speculative heredity claims.
